extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of philosophy and artists interested in aesthetic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and criteria for apprehending (enjoying) and producing genuine works of art, focusing on the required mental state (pure objectivity), what art must present (Ideas/species), and the physiological/psychological conditions that enable aesthetic perception and creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure objectivity of perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge turns away altogether from our own will and considers things as if they could never concern the will; the consciousness of other things (objective perception) becomes predominant and the consciousness of self vanishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This state is necessary for 'the enjoyment of æsthetic objects' and is the condition in which things appear with increased clearness and distinctness. It is not a voluntary act but arises from a temporary preponderance of the intellect over the will or strong excitation of the perceptive faculty without any excitement of desires or emotions. Physiological aids that favour it include a night of quiet sleep, a cold bath, calming the circulation, and avoiding spirituous drinks or opium. Anti-pattern: when the will regains the upper hand, perception is coloured by wishes, emotions, or cares and aesthetic purity is lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art facilitates apprehension of Ideas (art's objectivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Works of art (pictures, poetry) present objects outside all possibility of having any relation to the will and therefore appeal immediately to knowledge alone, making the apprehension of the Ideas easier than in reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because artistic objects exist 'only for knowledge' they secure the 'absolute silence of the will' required for pure objective comprehension. This is why pictures and poetry are especially effective at eliciting æsthetic satisfaction. Anti-pattern: attempting to apprehend Ideas through reality often requires abstraction from volition and is more difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art must spring from purely objective perception (production criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every good picture, poem, or genuine work 'bears the stamp of' a frame of mind in which perception is purely objective; genuine and original achievements grow from perception purified of volition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'punctum saliens' of great works— the vital incisive element— is a purely objective perception. For production, the intellect must free itself from service to the will so that the artist apprehends the Idea (species) rather than relations. Genius is the natural disposition enabling this. Anti-pattern: works produced from personal desire, utility, or mere relations lack this genuine germ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should express the Idea (species) not mere relations or utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic knowledge apprehends the 'essential' and therefore the whole species (Ideas) of a thing rather than mere relations (usefulness, end-directed features).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Idea is the 'complete and perfect phenomenon' that underlies relations; art's task is to reveal this permanent, unchanging form by eliminating the contingent relations. Anti-pattern: treating things primarily in terms of their function or relation to the perceiver reduces them to mere relations and prevents apprehension of the Idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterestedness (object must not concern the will)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty and æsthetic pleasure require that the perceived object 'does not concern us'—that perception be disinterested and outside personal relations to the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an object is unrelated to our wants or aversions, it appears beautiful; if it becomes related to our will, the beauty is immediately abolished (example: youthful longing that would ruin the present aesthetic charm). Anti-pattern: sensual passion or personal involvement turns aesthetic pleasure into desire or discomfort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of passion and personal involvement (passions distort perception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any emotion, inclination, or aversion disturbs and falsifies our knowledge and alters the original perception of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: fortunate events make the world look bright; cares make it gloomy; objects associated with abhorrent uses (scaffold, surgeon's instruments) appear hideous. Therefore aesthetic perception requires calmness and absence of passions. Anti-pattern: letting desire or aversion direct attention and colouring judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss (suspension) of individuality increases objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: With the disappearance of volition from consciousness the individuality also (and with it its suffering) is abolished; the perceiver becomes the 'pure subject of knowledge'—the 'eternal eye of the world'—and in that state perceives all things without burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This double existence (individual will vs. pure perceiver) means it is 'well' when one is the universal perceiver and 'ill' when one is exclusively individual. Anti-pattern: being 'in' a scene (actively involved) destroys the pure objectivity that makes art enjoyably beautiful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius as capacity for sustained objective apprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius consists in having a greater measure of the power of knowledge than is required for service of an individual will, so that surplus capacity becomes free to comprehend the world without reference to the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genius enables prolonged or higher-degree objective perception, making possible sustained production of works that apprehend Ideas. This is why artistic, poetic, and philosophical greatness often correlates with such capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty and estrangement increase picturesque/poetical effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects seen as strange or entirely novel to the perceiver favour purely objective apprehension and thus increase the picturesque or poetical impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the traveller perceives a strange town more agreeably than its inhabitants; transferring narrative/dramatic scenes to distant times or lands increases effect (Germany→Italy, etc.). Using unfamiliar settings helps produce the indifference to the will necessary for aesthetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should present essentials and eliminate the unessential
rubrics_metrics.description: Great art 'gives prominence to what is essential and eliminates what is unessential', thereby presenting things more distinctly and characteristically and facilitating apprehension of the Idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This selective distillation is part of why works of art have 'permanent worth' and continued approval: they express the purely objective element common across subjective variations. Anti-pattern: overburdening a work with contingent details tied to relations or utility blurs the Idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter preference: natural species over manufactured articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas (species) properly belong to natural things; manufactured articles have no Ideas but only conceptions (genera logica).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle's and Platonists' point: things produced by art (house, ring) do not possess Ideas in the same way that natural species do. For aesthetic work aiming at Ideas, natural objects and species are more apt subjects than artifacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apprehension of the Idea arises from perceiving many relations until the essential emerges
rubrics_metrics.description: When many and various relations of an object are apprehended, from these the peculiar and proper nature of the object appears more distinctly and gradually constructs itself out of mere relations into the Idea (species).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the cognitive route by which the intellect—once sufficiently detached from the will—arrives at the purely objective nature of a phenomenon. In practice, an artist or perceiver who notices multiple relations can abstract to the essential. Anti-pattern: stopping at superficial relations without synthesising them into the species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic satisfaction has two constituent elements: objectivity and relief from will
rubrics_metrics.description: One element is the pure objectivity of perception; the other is that with the withdrawal of the will from consciousness all possibility of suffering is abolished, so the state gives pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The state of pure knowing not only reveals Ideas but also produces pleasurable release because suffering (rooted in will) is absent. This explains why aesthetic contemplation is both illuminating and consoling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellect's deliverance from will must be temporary and non-volitional
rubrics_metrics.description: The intellect's emancipation from the service of the will is not a lasting emancipation but 'only a brief hour of rest', and it cannot be an act of the will (i.e., not produced by choice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hence moments of aesthetic perception are exceptional; their production depends on physiological and psychological conditions rather than deliberate willing. Anti-pattern: attempting to will oneself into pure objectivity.
